The AI world just split into two separate ecosystems — and most companies are not ready for it.

China announced a $295 billion five-year plan to build a fully sovereign AI infrastructure. Datacenters connected across the country. Huawei Ascend chips replacing NVIDIA at every level. 80% of all technology sourced domestically.

This is not a policy paper or a long-range aspiration. This is a funded, structured plan to build a parallel AI economy that operates without any dependence on Western silicon or cloud providers.

What does this mean for business leaders with global operations? If any part of your AI stack — training, inference, data pipelines — touches Chinese markets, Chinese partners, or Chinese regulatory requirements, you are heading toward a world where that infrastructure runs on entirely different hardware and software. Interoperability between these ecosystems is not guaranteed.

The companies that start building dual-stack AI strategies now will navigate this transition with optionality. The ones that assume a single global compute supply chain will be forced into reactive decisions when the split becomes operational.

The interconnect layer is the critical unknown — whether China adopts open optical standards or builds proprietary interconnects will determine how isolated or interoperable these two AI worlds ultimately become.
